Maladaptive Strategies.value: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

vignette: Saravanan is a 46-year-old South Eastern Asian male who has been married for over two decades. He works as a software engineer and has had a stable career until recently. Saravanan served in the military during his early twenties and experienced combat that left lasting psychological scars. The traumatic event occurred during a patrol mission when enemy forces ambushed their unit, resulting in intense gunfire and explosions. The smell of smoke and burnt rubber permeated the air, motorcycles revved as soldiers fled or pursued, and Saravanan had to disrobe at one point due to injuries from shrapnel. These specific elements have become potent triggers for his post-traumatic stress. Saravanan first noticed symptoms several weeks after returning home. The smell of smoke from a neighbor's barbecue reminded him vividly of the ambush, causing intense anxiety and panic attacks. This olfactory trigger led him to avoid going out, fearing he might encounter similar smells that would set off these distressing memories again. His avoidance extended to media consumption; watching films or TV shows with scenes reminiscent of combat heightened his emotional reactivity. The auditory recall of motorcycle noise became particularly disturbing. Once while working from home, a motorcycle passed by loudly outside his window, immediately transporting Saravanan back to that traumatic event. He heard the sounds vividly as if they were happening again, and this experience left him feeling on guard even inside his own home. As a result, he began to avoid familiar places and developed an aversion to going out in public. Saravanan also started experiencing intrusive memories that replayed like a film in his mind. He could not put the traumatic event into words; instead, these vivid, nonverbal recollections were triggered by even minor stimuli such as a loud noise or the sight of unfamiliar people walking past. These memories often led him to feel threatened by strangers and made it difficult for him to engage in activities he previously enjoyed, like exercising. The cycle of triggers, memories, and threat perception began to tighten over time. For instance, the auditory recall of combat sounds would lead Saravanan to withdraw further from his social life and avoid going out. This increased avoidance then intensified his feelings of vulnerability and heightened alertness at home, creating a self-perpetuating loop. Saravanan's work as a software engineer became affected by these symptoms. He found it increasingly difficult to concentrate on tasks and was constantly distracted by the memories that replayed in his mind. His tendency to avoid going out meant he missed important team meetings and social gatherings at the office, leading to strained relationships with colleagues. His wife noticed changes in Saravanan's behavior over time but did not understand the depth of his distress until he shared some details about his trauma. This sharing was a significant step for him; however, it also brought up more memories that replayed vividly, making it harder for him to avoid thinking about the traumatic event. Saravanan finally decided to seek help when his work performance deteriorated significantly and his wife expressed her concern over how his anxiety affected their relationship. He was most afraid of being overwhelmed by these intrusive memories again but also hoped that therapy could provide strategies to manage them more effectively, allowing him to regain control over his life. In summary, Saravanan’s experience is characterized by a complex interplay between triggers, maladaptive strategies, threat perception, and memory replay. Each element reinforces the others, creating a cycle of distress that has significantly impacted his daily functioning and well-being.
